Clinical Box 13–4 describes Horner syndrome, which is due to interruption of sympathetic nerves to the face. Clinical Box 13–5 describes a vasospastic condition (Raynaud phenomenon) in which blood flow to the fingers and toes is transiently reduced, typically when a sensitive individual is exposed to stress or cold. ++ CLINICAL BOX 13–2 Organophosphates: Pesticides and Nerve Gases The World Health Organization estimates that 1–3% of agricultural workers worldwide suffer from acute pesticide poisoning; it accounts for significant morbidity and mortality, especially in developing countries. Like organophosphate pesticides (eg, parathion and malathion), nerve gases (eg, soman and sarin) used in chemical warfare and terrorism inhibit acetylcholinesterase at peripheral and central cholinergic synapses, prolonging the actions of acetylcholine at these synapses. The organophosphate cholinesterase inhibitors are readily absorbed by the skin, lung, gut, and conjunctiva, making them very dangerous. They bind to the enzyme and undergo hydrolysis, resulting in a phosphorylated active site on the enzyme. The covalent phosphorous-enzyme bond is very stable and hydrolyzes at a very slow rate. The phosphorylated enzyme complex may undergo a process called aging in which one of the oxygen-phosphorous bonds breaks down, which strengthens the phosphorous-enzyme bond. This process takes only 10 min to occur after exposure to soman. The earliest signs of organophosphate toxicity are usually indicative of excessive activation of autonomic muscarinic receptors; these include miosis, salivation, sweating, bronchial constriction, vomiting, and diarrhea. CNS signs of toxicity include cognitive disturbances, convulsions, seizures, and even coma; these signs are often accompanied by nicotinic effects such as depolarizing neuromuscular blockade. THERAPEUTIC HIGHLIGHTS The muscarinic cholinergic receptor antagonist atropine is often given parenterally in large doses to control signs of excessive activation of muscarinic cholinergic receptors. When given soon after exposure to the organophosphate and before aging has occurred, nucleophiles such as pralidoxime are able to break the bond between the organophosphate and the acetylcholinesterase. Thus, this drug is called a "cholinesterase regenerator." If pyridostigmine is administered in advance of exposure to a cholinesterase inhibitor, it binds to the enzyme and prevents binding by the toxic organophosphate agent. The protective effects of pyridostigmine dissipate within 3–6 h, but this provides enough time for clearance of the organophosphate from the body. Since the drug cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, protection is limited to peripheral cholinergic synapses. A mixture of pyridostigmine, carbamate, and atropine can be administered prophylactically to soldiers and civilians who are at risk for exposure to nerve gases. Benzodiazepines can be used to abort the seizures caused by exposure to organophosphates. ++ CLINICAL BOX 13–3 Mushroom Poisoning Of more than 5000 species of mushrooms found in the United States, approximately 100 are poisonous and ingestion of about 12 of these can result in death. Estimates are an annual incidence of five cases per 100,000 individuals in the United States; worldwide databases are not available. Mushroom poisoning or mycetism is divided into rapid-onset (15–30 min after ingestion) and delayed-onset (6–12 h after ingestion) types. In rapid-onset cases caused by mushrooms of the Inocybe genus, the symptoms are due to excessive activation of muscarinic cholinergic synapses. The major signs of muscarinic poisoning include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, urinary urgency, vasodilation, sweating, and salivation. Ingestion of mushrooms such as the Amanita muscaria exhibit signs of the antimuscarinic syndrome rather than muscarinic poisoning because they also contain alkaloids that block muscarinic cholinergic receptors. The classic symptoms of this syndrome are being "red as a beet" (flushed skin), "hot as a hare" (hyperthermia), "dry as a bone" (dry mucous membranes, no sweating), "blind as a bat" (blurred vision and cycloplegia), and "mad as a hatter" (confusion and delirium). The delayed-onset type of mushroom poisoning occurs after ingestion of Amanita phalloides, Amanita virosa, Galerina autumnalis, and Galerina marginata. These mushrooms cause abdominal cramping, nausea, vomiting, and profuse diarrhea; but the major toxic effects are due to hepatic injury (jaundice and bruising) and associated central effects (confusion, lethargy, and coma). These mushrooms contain amatoxins that inhibit RNA polymerase. There is a 60% mortality rate associated with ingestion of these mushrooms. THERAPEUTIC HIGHLIGHTS The rapid-onset type muscarinic poisoning can be treated effectively with atropine. Individuals who exhibit the antimuscarinic syndrome can be treated with physostigmine, which is a cholinesterase inhibitor with a 2–4 h duration of action that acts centrally and peripherally. If agitated, these individuals may require sedation with a benzodiazepine or an antipsychotic agent. The delayed-onset of toxicity due to ingestion of mushrooms containing amatoxins does not respond to cholinergic drugs. Treatment of amatoxin ingestion includes intravenous administration of fluids and electrolytes to maintain adequate hydration. Administering a combination of a high-dose of penicillin G and silibinin (a flavonolignan found in certain herbs with antioxidant and hepatoprotective properties) has been shown to improve survival. If necessary, vomiting can also be induced by using activated charcoal to reduce the absorption of the toxin. ++ CLINICAL BOX 13–4 Horner Syndrome Horner syndrome is a rare disorder resulting from interruption of preganglionic or postganglionic sympathetic innervation to the face. The problem can result from injury to the nerves, injury to the carotid artery, a stroke or lesion in the brainstem, or a tumor in the lung. In most cases the problem is unilateral, with symptoms occurring only on the side of the damage. The hallmark of Horner syndrome is the triad of anhidrosis (reduced sweating), ptosis (drooping eyelid), and miosis (constricted pupil). Symptoms also include enophthalmos (sunken eyeball) and vasodilation. THERAPEUTIC HIGHLIGHTS There is no specific pharmacologic treatment for Horner syndrome, but drugs affecting noradrenergic neurotransmission can be used to determine whether the source of the problem is interruption of the preganglionic or postganglionic innervation to the face. Since the iris of the eye responds to topical sympathomimetic drugs (ie, drugs that are direct agonists on adrenoceptors or drugs that increase the release or prevent reuptake of norepinephrine from the nerve terminal), the clinician can easily test the viability of the noradrenergic nerves to the eye. If the postganglionic sympathetic fibers are damaged, their terminals would degenerate and there would be a loss of stored catecholamines. If the preganglionic fibers are damaged, the postganglionic noradrenergic nerve would remain intact (but be inactive) and would still have stored catecholamines in its terminal. If a drug that causes release of catecholamine stores (eg, hydroxyamphetamine) is administered and the constricted pupil does not dilate, one would conclude that the noradrenergic nerve is damaged. If the eye dilates in response to this drug, the catecholamine stores are still able to be released, so the damage must be preganglionic. Administration of phenylephrine (α-adrenoceptor agonist) would dilate the pupil regardless of the site of injury as the drug binds to the receptor on the radial muscle of the iris. ++ CLINICAL BOX 13–5 Raynaud Phenomenon Approximately 5% of men and 8% of women experience an episodic reduction in blood flow primarily to the fingers, often during exposure to cold or during a stressful situation. Vasospasms in the toes, tip of nose, ears, and penis can also occur. Smoking is associated with an increase in the incidence and severity of the symptoms of Raynaud phenomenon. The symptoms begin to occur between the age of 15 and 25; it is most common in cold climates. The symptoms often include a triphasic change in color of the skin of the digits. Initially, the skin becomes pale or white (pallor), cold, and numb. This can be followed by a cyanotic period in which the skin turns blue or even purple, during which time the reduced blood flow can cause intense pain. Once the blood flow recovers, the digits often turn deep red (rubor) and there can be swelling and tingling. Primary Raynaud phenomenon or Raynaud disease refers to the idiopathic appearance of the symptoms in individuals who do not have another underlying disease to account for the symptoms. In such cases, the vasospastic attacks may merely be an exaggeration of a normal response to cold temperature or stress. Secondary Raynaud phenomenon or Raynaud syndrome refers to the presence of these symptoms due to another disorder such as scleroderma, lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren syndrome, carpel tunnel syndrome, and anorexia. Although initially thought to reflect an increase in sympathetic activity to the vasculature of the digits, this is no longer regarded as the mechanism underlying the episodic vasospasms. THERAPEUTIC HIGHLIGHTS The first treatment strategy for Raynaud phenomenon is to avoid exposure to the cold, reduce stress, quit smoking, and avoid the use of medications that are vasoconstrictors (eg, β-adrenoceptor antagonists, cold medications, caffeine, and opioids). If the symptoms are severe, drugs may be needed to prevent tissue damage. These include calcium channel blockers (eg, nifedipine) and α-adrenoceptor antagonists (eg, prazosin). In individuals who do not respond to pharmacologic treatments, surgical sympathectomy has been done. +++ NONADRENERGIC & NONCHOLINERGIC TRANSMITTERS ++ In addition to the "classical neurotransmitters," some autonomic fibers also release neuropeptides, although their exact functions in autonomic control have not been determined. The small granulated vesicles in postganglionic noradrenergic neurons contain adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and norepinephrine, and the large granulated vesicles contain neuropeptide Y (NPY). There is some evidence that low-frequency stimulation promotes release of ATP, whereas high-frequency stimulation causes release of NPY. Some visceral organs contain purinergic receptors, and evidence is accumulating that ATP is a mediator in the ANS along with norepinephrine. ++ Many sympathetic fibers innervating the vasculature of viscera, skin, and skeletal muscles release NPY and galanin in addition to norepinephrine. Vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP), calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), or substance P are co-released with acetylcholine from the sympathetic innervation to sweat glands (sudomotor fibers). VIP is co-localized with acetylcholine in many cranial parasympathetic postganglionic neurons supplying glands. Vagal parasympathetic postganglionic neurons in the gastrointestinal tract contain VIP and the enzymatic machinery to synthesize nitric oxide (NO). + RESPONSES OF EFFECTOR ORGANS TO AUTONOMIC NERVE IMPULSES Download Section PDF Listen +++ +++ GENERAL PRINCIPLES ++ The ANS is responsible for regulating and coordinating many physiologic functions that include blood flow, blood pressure, heart rate, airflow through the bronchial tree, gastrointestinal motility, urinary bladder contraction, glandular secretions, pupillary diameter, body temperature, and sexual physiology. ++ The effects of stimulation of the noradrenergic and cholinergic postganglionic nerve fibers are indicated in Figure 13–3 and Table 13–1. These findings point out another difference between the ANS and the somatomotor nervous system. The release of acetylcholine by α-motor neurons only leads to contraction of skeletal muscles. In contrast, release of acetylcholine onto smooth muscle of some organs leads to contraction (eg, walls of the gastrointestinal tract) while release onto other organs promotes relaxation (eg, sphincters in the gastrointestinal tract). The only way to relax a skeletal muscle is to inhibit the discharges of the α-motor neurons; but for some targets innervated by the ANS, contraction can be shifted to relaxation by switching from activation of the parasympathetic nervous system to activation of the sympathetic nervous system. This is the case for the many organs that receive dual innervation with antagonistic effects, including the digestive tract, airways, and urinary bladder. The heart is another example of an organ with dual antagonistic control. Stimulation of sympathetic nerves increases heart rate; stimulation of parasympathetic nerves decreases heart rate. ++ In other cases, the effects of sympathetic and parasympathetic activation can be considered complementary. An example is the innervation of salivary glands. Parasympathetic activation causes release of watery saliva, while sympathetic activation causes the production of thick, viscous saliva. ++ The two divisions of the ANS can also act in a synergistic or cooperative manner in the control of some functions. One example is the control of pupil diameter in the eye. Both sympathetic and parasympathetic innervations are excitatory, but the former contracts the radial (or dilator) muscle to cause mydriasis (widening of the pupil) and the latter contracts the sphincter (or constrictor) muscle to cause miosis (narrowing of the pupil). Another example is the synergistic actions of these nerves on sexual function. Activation of parasympathetic nerves to the penis increases penile blood flow and leads to erection while activation of sympathetic nerves to the male reproductive tract causes ejaculation. ++ There are also several organs that are innervated by only one division of the ANS. In addition to the adrenal gland, most blood vessels, the pilomotor muscles in the skin (hair follicles), and sweat glands are innervated exclusively by sympathetic nerves (sudomotor fibers). The lacrimal muscle (tear gland), ciliary muscle (for accommodation for near vision), and the nasopharyngeal gland are innervated exclusively by parasympathetic nerves. +++ PARASYMPATHETIC, CHOLINERGIC, & SYMPATHETIC NORADRENERGIC DISCHARGE ++ In a general way, the functions promoted by activity in the cholinergic division of the ANS are those concerned with the vegetative aspects of day-to-day living. For example, parasympathetic action favors digestion and absorption of food by increasing the activity of the intestinal musculature, increasing gastric secretion, and relaxing the pyloric sphincter. For this reason, the cholinergic division is sometimes called the anabolic nervous system or the "rest and digest" division of the ANS. ++ The sympathetic (noradrenergic) division discharges as a unit in emergency situations and can be called the catabolic nervous system or the "flight or fight" division of the ANS. The effect of this discharge prepares the individual to cope with an emergency. Sympathetic activity dilates the pupils (letting more light into the eyes), accelerates the heartbeat and raises the blood pressure (providing better perfusion of the vital organs and muscles), and constricts the blood vessels of the skin (which limits bleeding from wounds). Noradrenergic discharge also leads to elevated plasma glucose and free fatty acid levels (supplying more energy). On the basis of effects like these, Walter Cannon called the emergency-induced discharge of the sympathetic nervous system the "preparation for flight or fight." ++ The emphasis on mass discharge in stressful situations should not obscure the fact that the sympathetic fibers also subserve other functions and, in fact, there is activity in sympathetic nerves even under resting conditions. For example, tonic sympathetic discharge to the arterioles maintains arterial pressure, and variations in this tonic discharge are the mechanism by which carotid sinus feedback regulation of blood pressure occurs (see Chapter 32). In addition, sympathetic discharge is decreased in fasting animals and increased when fasted animals are again fed. These changes may explain the decrease in blood pressure and metabolic rate produced by fasting and the opposite changes produced by feeding. + DESCENDING INPUTS TO AUTONOMIC PREGANGLIONIC NEURONS Download Section PDF Listen +++ ++ As is the case for α-motor neurons, the activity of autonomic nerves is dependent on both reflexes (eg, baroreceptor and chemoreceptor reflexes) and a balance between descending excitatory and inhibitory inputs from several brain regions. To identify brain regions that provide input to preganglionic sympathetic neurons, neuroanatomic tract tracing chemicals can be injected into the thoracic IML. These chemicals are picked up by axon terminals and transported retrogradely to the cell bodies of origin. Figure 13–5 shows the source of some forebrain and brainstem inputs to sympathetic preganglionic neurons. There are parallel pathways from the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus, pontine catecholaminergic A5 cell group, rostral ventrolateral medulla, and medullary raphe nuclei. This is analogous to projections from the brainstem and cortex converging on somatomotor neurons in the spinal cord. The rostral ventrolateral medulla is generally considered to major source of excitatory input to sympathetic neurons. In addition to these direct pathways to preganglionic neurons, there are many brain regions that feed into these pathways, including the amygdala, mesencephalic periaqueductal gray, caudal ventrolateral medulla, nucleus of the tractus solitarius, and medullary lateral tegmental field. This is analogous to the control of somatomotor function by areas such as the basal ganglia and cerebellum. Chapter 32 describes the role of some of these brain regions as well as the role of various reflexes in setting the level of activity in autonomic nerves supplying cardiovascular effector organs. ++ FIGURE 13–5 Pathways that control autonomic responses. Direct projections (solid lines) to autonomic preganglionic neurons include the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus, pontine A5 cell group, rostral ventrolateral medulla, and medullary raphe. Graphic Jump LocationView Full Size||Download Slide (.ppt) +++ AUTONOMIC DYSFUNCTION ++ Drugs, neurodegenerative diseases, trauma, inflammatory processes, and neoplasia are a few examples of factors that can lead to dysfunction of the ANS (Clinical Boxes 13–1, 13–2, 13–3, 13–4). The types of dysfunction can range from complete autonomic failure to autonomic hyperactivity. Among disorders associated with autonomic failure are orthostatic hypotension, neurogenic syncope (vasovagal response), erectile dysfunction, neurogenic bladder, gastrointestinal dysmotility, sudomotor failure, and Horner syndrome. Autonomic hyperactivity can be the basis for neurogenic hypertension, cardiac arrhythmias, neurogenic pulmonary edema, myocardial injury, hyperhidrosis, hyperthermia, and hypothermia. + ENTERIC NERVOUS SYSTEM Download Section PDF Listen +++ ++ The enteric nervous system, which can be considered as the third division of the ANS, is located within the wall of the digestive tract, all the way from the esophagus to the anus. It is composed of two well-organized neural plexuses. The myenteric plexus is located between longitudinal and circular layers of muscle; it is involved in control of digestive tract motility. The submucosal plexus is located between the circular muscle and the luminal mucosa; it senses the environment of the lumen and regulates gastrointestinal blood flow and epithelial cell function. ++ The enteric nervous system contains as many neurons as the entire spinal cord. It is sometimes referred to as a "mini-brain" as it contains all the elements of a nervous system including sensory neurons, interneurons, and motor neurons. It contains sensory neurons innervating receptors in the mucosa that respond to mechanical, thermal, osmotic, and chemical stimuli. Motor neurons control motility, secretion, and absorption by acting on smooth muscle and secretory cells. Interneurons integrate information from sensory neurons and feedback to the enteric motor neurons. ++ Parasympathetic and sympathetic nerves connect the CNS to the enteric nervous system or directly to the digestive tract. Although the enteric nervous system can function autonomously, normal digestive function often requires communication between the CNS and the enteric nervous system (see Chapter 25). + CHAPTER SUMMARY Download Section PDF Listen +++ ++ Preganglionic sympathetic neurons are located in the IML of the thoracolumbar spinal cord and project to postganglionic neurons in the paravertebral or prevertebral ganglia or the adrenal medulla. Preganglionic parasympathetic neurons are located in motor nuclei of cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X and the sacral IML. Postganglionic nerve terminals are located in smooth muscle (eg, blood vessels, gut wall, and urinary bladder), cardiac muscle, and glands (eg, sweat gland and salivary glands). Acetylcholine is released at nerve terminals of all preganglionic neurons, postganglionic parasympathetic neurons, and a few postganglionic sympathetic neurons (sweat glands and sympathetic vasodilator fibers). The remaining sympathetic postganglionic neurons release norepinephrine. Ganglionic transmission results from activation of nicotinic receptors. Postganglionic cholinergic transmission is mediated by activation of muscarinic receptors. Postganglionic adrenergic transmission is mediated by activation of α1-, β-, or β2-adrenoceptors, depending on the target organ. Many common drugs exert their therapeutic actions by serving as agonists or antagonists at autonomic synapses. Sympathetic activity prepares the individual to cope with an emergency by accelerating the heartbeat, raising blood pressure (perfusion of the vital organs), and constricting the blood vessels of the skin (limits bleeding from wounds). Parasympathetic activity is concerned with the vegetative aspects of day-to-day living and favors digestion and absorption of food by increasing the activity of the intestinal musculature, increasing gastric secretion, and relaxing the pyloric sphincter. Direct projections to sympathetic preganglionic neurons in the IML originate in the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus, pontine catecholaminergic A5 cell group, rostral ventrolateral medulla, and medullary raphe nuclei. Based on the evidence gathered, the muscarinic backup mechanism in sympathetic ganglionic transmission appears to be **activity-dependent**, and while specific receptor subtypes (particularly M1 and M2) have been identified in this pathway, their exact roles vary between ganglia and species. Here’s a detailed synthesis:

---

### **1. Activity-Dependency of Muscarinic Transmission**

The evidence suggests that muscarinic transmission in sympathetic ganglia is not constitutive but is recruited especially during high-frequency stimulation. In the stellate ganglion, preganglionic stimulation at high frequency enhanced the responsiveness of ganglion cells to acetylcholine and other agonists, though not to nicotinic stimuli like nicotine. This indicates that muscarinic mechanisms become more prominent under conditions of increased neuronal activity, effectively providing a “backup” when nicotinic transmission is compromised or during high-frequency firing.

This aligns with the broader model in document 542311781, where muscarinic and peptidergic receptors mediate **slow and late slow excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs)** that facilitate the transmission of high-frequency impulses through the primary nicotinic pathway. Essentially, during periods of intense preganglionic activity, muscarinic receptors are engaged to modulate and sustain transmission, making the system more resilient.

---

### **2. Muscarinic Receptor Subtypes in Sympathetic Ganglia**

The literature consistently identifies **M1 and M2 receptors** as key players in sympathetic ganglionic transmission, but their functions differ:

- **M1 receptors** are primarily involved in generating the **slow EPSP**. They are linked to Gq proteins and reduce potassium permeability, leading to depolarization. In the superior cervical ganglion, M1 receptors mediate the slow excitatory response that follows the initial fast nicotinic EPSP.

- **M2 receptors** are associated with the **slow inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP)**. They are coupled to Gi proteins, which open potassium channels and hyperpolarize the neuron. In the stellate ganglion, M2 activation produces an IPSP after the initial nicotinic response.

Document 410667429 explicitly describes this sequence: a fast EPSP (nicotinic) → IPSP (M2) → slow EPSP (M1) → possibly a peptide-induced EPSP. This multiphasic response allows fine-tuning of ganglionic transmission.

---

### **3. Regional Specificity and Open Questions**

While M1 and M2 are well-documented in ganglia like the superior cervical and stellate ganglia, less direct evidence exists for the **greater splanchnic nerve pathway** and celiac ganglion. However, given the conserved nature of autonomic ganglionic transmission, similar mechanisms likely apply. The greater splanchnic nerve arises from thoracic segments T5–T9 and synapses at the celiac plexus, which is part of the sympathetic prevertebral ganglia. These ganglia share similar receptor profiles with other sympathetic ganglia, though subtype distributions may vary.

Some caveats and open questions remain:
- **Species differences**: Most data come from rodent or feline models; human ganglionic circuitry may differ.
- **Functional heterogeneity**: Not all ganglion cells respond identically. In the stellate ganglion, muscarinic transmission persists to adrenergic neurons even after nicotinic blockade, but not to cholinergic neurons.
- **Presynaptic vs. postsynaptic roles**: Muscarinic receptors can also modulate transmitter release presynaptically (e.g., M2 autoreceptors), adding complexity.

---

### **4. Synthesis and Future Directions**

The muscarinic backup in sympathetic ganglia is **activity-dependent**, recruited during high-frequency stimulation to enhance transmission via slow EPSPs (M1) and modulate excitability via slow IPSPs (M2). This mechanism ensures robust signaling under demanding conditions, such as stress or sustained sympathetic outflow.

For the greater splanchnic nerve and celiac ganglion, the evidence is extrapolated from other sympathetic ganglia but is plausible given the conserved anatomy. Future research should focus on:
- Direct electrophysiological studies in celiac ganglion neurons.
- Clarifying whether M3 or other subtypes play roles in specific pathways.
- Investigating species-specific differences in receptor expression.

In summary, muscarinic transmission in sympathetic ganglia is a dynamic, activity-dependent process primarily mediated by M1 (excitatory) and M2 (inhibitory) receptors, offering a backup route when nicotinic transmission is insufficient.

The Spinal Nerves - ScienceDirect A Christopher and Dana Reeve Foundation Text and Atlas 2009, Pages 37-56 Chapter 4 - The Spinal Nerves Gulgun Kayalioglu https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-374247-6.50008-0 Get rights and content The anatomy of the dorsal and ventral roots and spinal nerves The spinal nerves transmit sensory information from the target organs to the central nervous system, and send motor commands from the central nervous system to muscles and target organs. Along the entire length of the spinal cord, spinal nerves arise at regular intervals and leave the vertebral column between the adjacent vertebrae through the intervertebral foramina. In humans there are 31 pairs of spinal nerves: 8 cervical (C1-C8), 12 thoracic (T1-T12), 5 lumbar (L1-L5), 5 sacral (S1-S5) and 1 coccygeal (Co1). There are 34 pairs of spinal nerves in the rat (8 cervical, 13 thoracic, 6 lumbar, 4 sacral, and 3 coccygeal) and 38 pairs (8 cervical, 13 thoracic, 7 lumbar, 3 sacral, and 7 coccygeal) in the cat. In humans, the first seven cervical spinal nerves emerge from the vertebral canal above their respective vertebrae, the remainder all emerge from below their respective vertebrae. The nerve emerging between C7 and T1 is named the eighth cervical nerve to link the two arrangements. The human cervical nerves increase in size from C1 to C6 and the size stays constant from C7 to T1. Thoracic spinal nerves from T2 to T12 are small and similar in size. Lumbar spinal nerves are large, their size increasing from L1 to L5. The largest spinal nerve is S1, after that the sacral nerves become smaller. The coccygeal nerve is the smallest spinal nerve. Each spinal nerve is attached to the spinal cord by a ventral (anterior) and a dorsal (posterior) root. Each root is formed by six to eight rootlets that extend throughout the whole length of the corresponding spinal cord segment. The ventral rootlets are made up of axons of motor neurons and dorsal rootlets are made up of the axons of sensory neurons. Each dorsal nerve root bears a dorsal root (spinal) ganglion, the cells of which give rise to peripheral and central nerve fibers. Because of the difference in length between the spinal cord and the vertebral column (the vertebral column is about 20% longer than the spinal cord), the length of the nerve roots increases progressively from rostral to caudal, and the rootlets run more vertically in the caudal segments. The lumbosacral nerve roots form the cauda equina below the termination of the spinal cord. The pia mater and the arachnoid mater cover the dorsal and ventral roots until they pierce the dura. After that, they receive a dural sheath, which continues with the epineurium of the spinal nerve (see Figures 4.1 and 4.2 ). Figure 4.1. Dorsal and ventral roots of spinal nerves This is a photograph of a dissection showing the ventral surface of the spinal cord and the ventral and dorsal rootlets. Groups of rootlets form the dorsal and ventral roots of each spinal nerve. The dura and arachnoid have been removed to expose the spinal cord. (Photograph courtesy of Professor Mete Erturk, Ege University). Figure 4.2. Transverse section of cord and meninges This diagram shows the relationship between the spinal cord and the three meningeal layers – pia mater, arachnoid mater, and dura mater. The dura mater is separated from the surrounding bone by a layer of fat, in which vertebral veins are embedded. The denticulate ligament can be seen projecting from the pia mater. The swelling of the dorsal root ganglion can be seen lying in the intervertebral canal. (Adapted from Moore and Dalley, 2006, p.524) Copyright © 2006 At the attachment point of each rootlet to the spinal cord, there is a transition zone between the central nervous system and the peripheral nervous system; this zone is used extensively to study axon regeneration. Here, the central and peripheral nervous tissues are separated by an irregular but clearly defined interface that consists of astrocytic tissue. Myelin sheaths are formed by oligodendrocytes on the central side of this interface and by Schwann cells on the peripheral side. The central nervous system-peripheral nervous system transitional zone is penetrated only by axons (Fraher, 2000 ). Thick myelinated fibers in the dorsal rootlet become directed to the center of the rootlet, whereas thinly myelinated and unmyelinated fibers are positioned at the periphery, concentrated on the ventrolateral zone of the rootlet in the transition zone (Carlstedt et al., 2004 ). Intradural intersegmental connections may be present between the dorsal or ventral rootlets and the adjacent dorsal root ganglia (Jacob and Weddell, 1975; Parke and Watanabe, 1987 ). Connections between dorsal rootlets occur most frequently in the cervical region (61%) in humans, compared to 7% in thoracic and 22% in lumbar segments. Similar connections between ventral rootlets have also been noticed but are less frequent (10% in the cervical and 5% in the lumbar segments). No connections have been observed between thoracic ventral rootlets (Moriishi et al., 1989 ). These connections usually occur by means of a peripheral dorsal or a ventral rootlet converging at the spinal cord surface and forming an irregular group of ectopic rootlets that join the central portion of the next rostral or caudal rootlet (Parke and Watanabe, 1987 ). Connections between dorsal rootlets may provide a pathway for overlap of sensory dermatomes and motor innervation of the limbs and trunk (Marzo et al., 1987 ). Within spinal nerves, there may be somatic sensory fibers from the skin and musculoskeletal system, visceral afferent fibers, motor fibers to voluntary striated muscles, sympathetic fibers to blood vessels and glands, and parasympathetic fibers to pelvic visceral organs. Each of these fiber types has a precise source or destination within the spinal cord. Each ventral root (also named the anterior root, radix anterior, radix ventralis, or radix motoria) is attached to the spinal cord by a series of rootlets that emerge from the ventrolateral sulcus of the spinal cord. Unlike the dorsal root fibers that are arranged in a neat line at their emergence from the spinal cord, ventral root fibers form an elliptical area named the anterior root exit zone (AREZ). The ventral roots predominantly consist of efferent somatic motor fibers (thick alpha motor axons and medium-sized gamma motor axons) derived from nerve cells of the ventral column. In thoracic and upper lumbar segments, these are supplemented by thin autonomic preganglionic motor fibers derived from the intermediolateral column. Injury filling of the ventral roots with HRP results in labelling of autonomic preganglionic neurons and their dendritic arbors, indicating there are also afferent fibers terminating on autonomic preganglionic neurons in the ventral roots of cat sacral spinal cord (Mawe et al., 1984; 1986 ). Unmyelinated sensory afferent fibers innervating the ventral root and its pial sheath have also been shown electrophysiologically in the cat sacral spinal cord (Jãnig and Koltzenburg, 1991 ). Most of the ventral root fibers are myelinated, but there are also unmyelinated C fibers the majority of which are autonomic. In the rat, cat, mouse and monkey, ventral roots of C1-C8 and L3-S1 segments, which are outside the autonomic (thoracolumbar) outflow, contain C fibers (Clifton et al., 1976; Coggeshall and Ito, 1977; Coggeshall et al., 1977; Biscoe et al., 1982; Chung and Kang, 1987; Karlsson et al., 1991 ). A significant number (25%) of fibers in human ventral roots are C fibers. It is proposed that a significant fraction of these are sensory afferents (Coggeshall et al., 1975; Hosobuchi, 1980 ). This has been confirmed by electrophysiological studies on C fibers in the cat ventral root (Clifton et al., 1976 ). If so, this may explain the failure of dorsal rhizotomy to relieve chronic pain (Coggeshall, 1979 ). However, the immunohistochemical and electron microscopic studies on this matter are contradictory. Substance P and/or calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) containing axons are found in ventral roots of the mouse (Kimura et al., 1994 ), rat (Karlsson and Hildebrand, 1996 ), cat (Risling et al., 1984) and monkey (Hegde et al., 1988 ), but it has been shown that these do not enter the spinal cord via the ventral roots (Risling et al., 1984, 1994; Kimura et al., 1994; Karlsson and Hildebrand, 1996 ). According to the available evidence, the presence of unmyelinated fibers in the ventral roots is explained as follows: afferent fibers from the periphery project into the central nervous system using ventral roots as a pathway to the spinal cord; afferent ventral root fibers innervate the ventral spinal pia mater and/or the ventral root itself and enter the cord via dorsal roots; afferent fibers course into the ventral root from the periphery but loop back and enter the spinal cord via the dorsal root; peripheral afferents, which lack a dorsal root projection, course into the ventral root where they diminish gradually; alternatively, these unmyelinated fibers in the ventral root are blindly ending third projections of the peripheral afferent fibers entering the central nervous system via a dorsal root (Hildebrand et al., 1997; Karlsson and Zakrisson, 1998 ). Ventral roots The number of ventral root axons increases gradually along its subarachnoid course to the point it is apposed to the dorsal root ganglion. This increase is probably due to axonal sprouting (branching) (Fraher and O'Sullivan, 1989 ). Axon numbers also change during maturation and throughout maturity. In the rat, the number of axons slightly increases immediately after birth, but after that there is a sharp decline between 4 to 20 days due to a marked loss of unmyelinated axons. A gradual decline in the number of myelinated axons continues up to 500 days (Fraher and O'Sullivan, 1989 ). An increase in the number of unmyelinated axons in ventral roots has also been shown to occur postnatally in the cat, and it is proposed that this results from axonal sprouting (Risling et al., 1981 ). Dorsal roots and primary afferent projections to the spinal cord Each dorsal root (also named the posterior root, radix posterior, radix dorsalis or radix sensoria) is attached to the dorsolateral sulcus of the spinal cord by a series of rootlets arranged in a line – the dorsal root entry zone (DREZ). In humans, there are 31 pairs of dorsal roots; the dorsal root of C1 spinal nerve is very small, and occasionally absent. Dorsal roots are larger than the ventral roots with thicker and more numerous fibers. In the cervical region of humans, the average number of dorsal rootlets range from 6.7 to 8.7 from C3 to T1, and the length of the DREZ varies from 10.7 mm at C7 to 12.7 mm at C4 (Alleyne et al., 1998 ). Each dorsal root fiber is the central process of a dorsal root ganglion cell. The dorsal roots contain sensory fibers from the skin, subcutaneous and deep tissues, and viscera. Primary afferent fibers of the dorsal roots are either myelinated or unmyelinated. Cutaneous, joint and visceral afferents are composed of myelinated Aα/β, Aδ and unmyelinated C fibers. Afferent fibers from muscles are also myelinated (group I, II, III fibers) and unmyelinated (group IV fibers). No efferent fibers have been shown to be present in the dorsal roots. There are also some unmyelinated nerve fibers that do not reach the spinal cord, terminating blindly within the dorsal roots (Carlstedt, 1977 ). It is estimated that there are 2-2.5 million afferent fibers in human adult dorsal roots on each side (Schoenen and Grant, 2004 ). Although former studies suggest the number of dorsal root axons is considerably larger than the number of dorsal root ganglion neurons, possibly due to sprouting of dorsal root axons (Langford and Coggeshall, 1979; Chung and Coggeshall, 1984 ), a recent stereological study by Tandrup (1995) demonstrated that there is a 1:1 ratio of dorsal root fibers to neurons in the dorsal root ganglion. In the DREZ, thin unmyelinated and thick myelinated fibers are located in the lateral and medial parts of the dorsal root, respectively (Light and Perl, 1979 ). Unmyelinated C fibers usually assemble into Remak bundles in the peripheral nervous system, where they are isolated from one another by cytoplasmic processes of Schwann cells. The dorsal roots are an exception to this, here about 7% to 9% of axons are immediately adjacent to other axons (Murinson and Griffin, 2004 ). Neuronal tracers, in particular HRP, have been widely used in the rat and cat to study the terminations of primary afferent projections in the spinal cord. Thin unmyelinated fibers reach the spinal cord within the lateral part of the dorsal roots and enter the dorsal horn by way of the dorsolateral fasciculus (Lissauer's tract) to terminate in superficial laminae (laminae 1-2) of the dorsal horn. Thick myelinated fibers enter the spinal cord within the medial part of the dorsal roots and project into the deep layers of dorsal horn and the ventral horn. There are exceptions to this rule, as thin unmyelinated fibers are also observed in laminae 5, 7 and 10 (Schouenborg, 1984; Sugiura et al., 1989; Mizumura et al., 1993 ). Terminal branches of C-fibers of somatic and visceral origin are distributed mainly in laminae 1-2 in the guinea pig (Sugiura et al., 1993 ). Cutaneous nociceptive afferents terminate mainly in laminae 1-3 (Maslany et al., 1992 ), large Aβ fibers from cutaneous mechanoreceptors terminate in laminae 3-5 (Woolf, 1987 ). Afferents from hair follicles descend through laminae 1-3 to laminae 4-5, then curve back to end in the superficial part of lamina 4 and lamina 3 (Brown et al., 1977 ). Visceral afferent fibers are composed of mainly unmyelinated C fibers and thin myelinated Aδ fibers, although a population of small rapidly conducting myelinated fibers is also present (Knuepfer and Schramm, 1987; Vera and Nadelhaft, 1990 ). Their terminations are mainly in laminae 1 and 5 (Cervero and Connell, 1984; Sugiura et al., 1993 ). The distribution of primary afferents in Rexed's laminae and specific nuclei of the spinal cord are discussed in Chapter 6. There is also a somatotopic arrangement for the termination of primary afferents on dorsal horn neurons, spinal nerves terminating on characteristic regions in the dorsal horn, distal parts of the limbs represented medially and proximal parts represented laterally (Ygge and Grant, 1983; Molander and Grant, 1985; 1987; Swett and Woolf, 1985; Shortland and Woolf, 1993 ). However, there is a similar spinal projection pattern for different muscle nerves, suggesting either a less developed or an essentially different somatotopic organization for muscle afferents compared to cutaneous afferents, as revealed in earlier studies (Molander and Grant, 1987 ). Dorsolateral fasciculus (Lissauer's tract) The dorsolateral fasciculus, first described by Lissauer (1885), is a small bundle of fibers running longitudinally in the white matter between the dorsolateral edge of the dorsal horn and the surface of the spinal cord. Small myelinated Ad and C primary afferent fibers enter the dorsolateral fasciculus. Axons of the dorsal horn neurons are also observed here (Coggeshall et al., 1981 ). Most of these fibers enter the substantia gelatinosa at or near the level of their origin, only some ascend or descend for a few segments (Traub et al., 1986 ). In the rat, the majority of the axons in the dorsolateral fasciculus at mid-thoracic and lumbosacral levels are primary afferent fibers, a slightly higher percentage of the fibers are unmyelinated, as opposed to the myelinated fibers (Chung et al., 1979 ). In the monkey, about 40% of the axons in the dorsolateral fasciculus are primary afferent axons from a single segment, and about another 40% are primary afferents from neighbouring cranial and caudal segments, the remaining 20% are propriospinal axons (Coggeshall et al., 1981 ). Each dorsal spinal root bears an ovoid swelling named the dorsal root (spinal) ganglion (DRG). The DRG is located close to the junction of the dorsal and ventral roots. On either side of the DRG, there may be scattered or grouped neurons particularly in the dorsal roots of the lumbar and sacral nerves, named the aberrant spinal ganglion cells. These are DRG neurons displaced during the growth process. The DRG cells are primary sensory neurons. They are pseudo-unipolar neurons with a single axon that after a short course divides into a peripheral and a central branch. The central branch enters the spinal cord via the dorsal roots and carries information from the cell body of DRG neuron to the spinal cord. The peripheral branch conveys sensory information from the body to the DRG cell body. Electron microscopic studies in the rat have shown that these two branches are not formed by the fusion of two opposite processes (as was once thought), but are both derived from the elongated cytoplasm of the cell body (Takahashi and Ninomiya, 1987 ). The DRG is encapsulated in a condensed connective tissue that is continuous with the sheath of the peripheral nerves. Dorsal root (spinal) ganglia The DRG neurons start developing as early as the ventral horn neurons, at 7 weeks of gestation (Kato and Takashima, 1994 ). As their appearance is before the development of osseous spine components, DRGs vary in orientation and location in different segments of the spine (Khorooshi et al., 2001 ). In the adult human, DRGs lie along the vertebral column within the intervertebral foramina. The exception to this are the DRGs of the first and second cervical nerves, which lie upon the vertebral arches of the atlas and axis, and the DRGs of the second to fifth sacral nerves and that of the coccygeal nerve, which lie within the vertebral canal (see Figure 4.3 ). (Adapted from Cramer and Darby, 2005, p.79) Copyright © 2005 The first DRG, together with the dorsal root, is either reduced in size or absent. The C2 DRG is proximally placed and occupies most of the foramen height, which may render it vulnerable to entrapment (Lu and Ebraheim, 1998 ). The C7 DRG is more distally situated within the intervertebral foramen C7 when compared to C6 (Yabuki and Kikuchi, 1996 ). Thoracic DRGs lie within the intervertebral foramina. Most of the lumbar DRGs are located within the intervertebral foramina, with only about 6% in the vertebral canal. The human lumbar DRGs gradually increase in size from L1 to L5, the width increasing from 3.7 mm to 5.9 mm, the length increasing from 4.3 to 9.4 mm, and the height increasing from 4.3 to 8.3 mm (Hasegawa et al., 1996 ). Double ganglia (biganglia) are frequently observed in L3 and L4 (Shen et al., 2006 ). The upper sacral DRGs are located within the intervertebral foramina, 55-60% in S1 and 15-50% in S2; the remainder lie within the vertebral canal. All S3 and S4 DRGs are located in the vertebral canal. The S1 DRG is larger than other sacral ganglia (Ebraheim and Lu, 1998 ). The coccygeal DRGs are located within the vertebral canal, sometimes in the form of scattered nerve cells rather than a swelling. DRG neurons are divided into two histological types called ′small, dark′ and ′large, light′ based on their staining properties seen through light microscopy (Lawson, 1979 ). The large, light DRG cells are rich in neurofilaments, whereas the small, dark neurons are poor in neurofilaments (Lawson et al., 1984; Holford et al., 1994 ). Electron microscopic studies have classified the large light cells as A cells and the small dark cells as B cells. A detailed electron microscopic study by Rambourg et al., (1983) defined three types of cells (A, B, C) on the basis of their size and distribution of organelles. They were able to further divide into six subtypes on the basis of the arrangement and organization of Nissl bodies and Golgi apparatus. Large light DRG cells give rise to myelinated Aa and Aβ fibers and small-myelinated mechanoreceptive Ad fibers; the small dark cells give rise to nociceptive Ad and unmyelinated C fibers (Bergman et al., 1999 ). The cells of origin of Ad fibers are larger when compared to those of C fibers (Harper and Lawson, 1985; Tandrup, 1995 ). However in the cat, unmyelinated afferent fibers do not originate exclusively from the smallest DRG cells but from the whole cell size spectrum (Hoheisel and Mense, 1986 ). The small dark cells that give rise to nociceptive fibers contain peptidergic neurotransmitters such as substance P, galanin, leu-enkephalin, CGRP, vasoactive intestinal polypeptide, cholecystokinin and somatostatin (Hayashi et al., 1983; Salt and Hill, 1983; Ju et al., 1987; Garry et al., 1989; Lawson et al., 1993 ). More neuronal profiles are labeled for substance P in human (44%) than in rat (20%) (Holford et al., 1994 ). DRG neurons also contain acetylcholine (Sann et al., 1995; Tata et al., 2004) and express both nicotinic and muscarinic receptors (Bernardini et al., 1998, 1999; Genzen et al., 2001 ). Vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT) has been shown preferentially in medium/large-sized neurons and muscarinic receptors in small to medium-sized neurons and in glial cells (Bernardini et al., 1998, 1999; Tata et al., 2004 ). The expression of cholinergic markers in DRG neurons starts at early developmental stages, increases gradually and reaches a peak in adulthood (Tata et al., 1994; Biagioni et al., 1999 ). Some small dark DRG neurons are catecholaminergic, containing tyrosine hydroxylase (Price and Mudge, 1983; Price, 1985 ). Although some peptides exist alone in a distinct subpopulation of neurons in the DRG, some are co-localized with other transmitter substances. It is suggested that in these neurons one neuropeptide is the main neurotransmitter and the other a neuromodulator regulating the functions of the main neurotransmitter (Ju et al., 1987; Cameron et al., 1988 ). Nitric oxide synthase immunoreactivity and/or NADPH-diaphorase reactivity has been shown in the thoracolumbar and lumbosacral DRGs of the rat, dog, cat, and guinea pig (Aimi et al., 1991; Vizzard et al., 1994; Zhou et al., 1998; Lukacova et al., 2006 ;). These neurons contain both substance P and CGRP (Aimi et al., 1991 ). Nitric oxide possibly has a neuroprotective effect on DRG neurons, and may facilitate regeneration (Thippeswamy and Morris, 2002 ). Most lumbar DRG cells are small, dark cells (Perry and Lawson, 1998; Bergman et al., 1999 ). In humans, the L5 DRG contains 11 000 large, 32 000 intermediate and 25 000 small neurons (Kawamura and Dyck, 1978 ). In resin-embedded sections in the rat, the number of neurons in C4-C6 DRGs was found to be 6800-7500 (Mille-Hamard et al., 1999 ). The L4, L5 and L6 DRG contained about 12 000, 15 000, and 14 000 neurons, respectively. In paraffin sections, where the small neurons are difficult to identify, the counts are 23% less (Schmalbruch, 1987 ). There is controversy on the alteration of the number of DRG neurons with age, probably depending on the species studied and the methodology used. Some studies report an increase in cell number, presumed to be due to neuron proliferation or to late differentiation of neurons that do not present a typical appearance until adulthood (Devor and Govrin-Lipmann, 1991; Popken and Farel, 1997 ). Others suggest that the total number remains constant during adult life (Aldskogius and Risling, 1989; Pover et al., 1994; Mohammed and Santer, 2001 ). A small decrease (12%) in the number of DRG neurons has also been reported in aged rats (Bergman and Ulfhake, 1998 ). A rostrocaudal organization in the DRG has been shown in the rat in relation to the formation of plexuses (Wessels et al., 1994 ). A columnar organization has been observed in the cat DRGs; neurons in the lateral border are connected to more rostral body parts, and neurons in the medial border are connected to more caudal body parts (Kausz and Rethelyi, 1985 ). No somatotopic organization is observed in the thoracic DRGs of the rat, but occasional clustering of labeled cells belonging to the same peripheral nerve was noted (Ygge, 1984 ). DRG neurons in the rat are arranged in pairs or, less frequently, in groups of three enclosed within a common connective sheath. Sometimes these nerve cell bodies are closely in contact with each other, and sometimes they are separated by neuroglial satellite cells (Pannese et al., 1991 ). The satellite cells rest on a basal lamina of connective tissue that is continuous with the endoneurium; these cells seem to provide metabolic support to DRG neurons. The number of satellite cells increases along with the volume of ganglion neurons with which they are associated (Ledda et al., 2004 ). The sympathetic fibers entering the DRG are vessel-associated fibers located between nerve fiber layers and around perikarya of DRG neurons (McLachlan et al., 1993 ). Primary sensory afferents have projections to spinal cord neurons that regulate the sympathetic outflow to the corresponding DRG. It has been suggested that imbalance in this circuit resulting from peripheral nerve injury might have a role in neuropathic pain (Hofstetter et al., 2005 ). Large DRG neurons relay low-threshold mechanical and proprioceptive stimuli, whereas small DRG neurons respond to high-threshold stimuli (Harper and Lawson, 1985 ). The ventral and dorsal roots join together and form the spinal nerve at each segmental level. The spinal nerve runs from the lateral aspect of the dural sac to the intervertebral foramen in a tubular canal of variable length; this canal is named the nerve root canal. Extensions of the dural sheath encase all nerve roots here as they depart from the dural sac (Gilchrist et al., 2002 ). Just lateral to the intervertebral foramen, each spinal nerve gives off a sinuvertebral (recurrent meningeal) branch that re-enters the vertebral canal. The sinuvertebral nerve is formed by a somatic root from a ventral ramus and an autonomic root from a neighbouring gray ramus communicans (Faustmann, 2004 ). The sinuvertebral nerve supplies the posterior longitudinal ligament, outer 1/3 part of anulus fibrosus, epidural blood vessels, ventral dura mater, dural sleeve, and the dorsal vertebral periosteum. After giving the sinuvertebral nerve, the spinal nerve immediately bifurcates into a small dorsal (posterior) ramus and a much larger ventral (anterior) ramus. The dorsal and ventral rami contain both motor and sensory fibers. Spinal nerves The axons of spinal nerves vary in diameter. Aa fibers are the largest (15-20 μm thick) and most heavily myelinated fibers that conduct action potentials most rapidly. Aβ fibers constitute the medium-sized and well-myelinated axons of Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles and Merkel discs. Thin, poorly myelinated mechanoreceptor fibers with large receptive fields form Ad fibers. C fibers are very thin, poorly conducting axons that terminate without capsules or other types of end organs in the skin (Zigmond et al., 1999 ). A cutaneous region innervated by a single spinal nerve is named a dermatome, and muscles innervated by a single spinal nerve as a myotome. Each spinal nerve contains somatic and visceral fibers that are further classified functionally as somatic afferent, somatic efferent, visceral afferent and visceral efferent fibers. The somatic afferent fibers are peripheral processes of DRG neurons that carry impulses generated by external stimulations and are known as exteroceptive fibers. These fibers carry sensory information from the skin, subcutaneous tissues, skeletal muscles, tendons, and joints. The somatic efferent fibers are axons of ventral horn neurons which carry motor impulses to the skeletal muscles. The visceral afferent fibers are composed of peripheral processes of DRG neurons that convey visceral sensation; these are known as interoceptive fibers. Visceral afferent fibers constitute less than 10% of afferent fibers in dorsal roots. The visceral efferent fibers are autonomic (sympathetic or parasympathetic) nerve fibers that carry motor impulses to the smooth and cardiac muscles and to the glands. Parasympathetic preganglionic efferent fibers originate from the neurons of the sacral parasympathetic nucleus (or the intermediolateral cell column) (for detailed information, see Chapter 8 ). Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers arise from the S2-S4 spinal cord segments in the human and cat (Brown and Nolan, 1979 ), and from the L6-S1 spinal cord segments in the rat (Nadelhaft and Booth, 1984 ). They leave the spinal cord by way of the ventral roots and pass into the corresponding spinal nerves. As the spinal nerve branches into dorsal and ventral rami, parasympathetic preganglionic fibers stay in the ventral rami. After they exit through the ventral sacral foramina they diverge from the ventral rami to form the pelvic splanchnic nerves. They pass through the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus to synapse in the terminal ganglia of pelvic parasympathetic ganglia. Sympathetic preganglionic efferent fibers originate from the intermediolateral cell column of the spinal cord of all thoracic and upper two or three lumbar spinal cord segments, and emerge by way of the corresponding ventral roots. These preganglionic efferent fibers constitute the thoracolumbar (autonomic) outflow. Sympathetic preganglionic axons have a small diameter (1.5-4 μm) and are myelinated, therefore appearing white in fresh specimens. In rats, unlike humans and cats, the great majority of preganglionic fibers are unmyelinated (Hedger and Webber, 1976 ). These axons soon leave the spinal nerve to form the white rami communicantes and enter the sympathetic chain. The sympathetic chain (also called the sympathetic trunk, paravertebral chain) is composed of gangliated cords running down along the length of the vertebral column on each side, extending from the skull base to the coccyx. In the human, each sympathetic chain consists of a series of 22 paravertebral ganglia: 3 cervical, 11 thoracic, 4 lumbar, and 4 sacral. The rat sympathetic chain consists of 3 cervical, 10 thoracic, 6 lumbar, 4 sacral and 1 caudal paravertebral ganglia on each side. In the cat, there are 3 cervical and 13 thoracic sympathetic ganglia; the lumbar sympathetic chain consists of 7 ganglia interconnected by nerve fibers (Wischnitzer, 1967 ). The fibers entering the paravertebral ganglia synapse with ganglionic neurons at the same level, or after ascending or descending for several segments. Neurons that lie rostrally within a spinal cord segment tend to project rostrally, and neurons lying caudally project caudally in the sympathetic chain (Forehand et al., 1994 ). Some fibers synapse with more than one ganglionic neuron via collateral branches (Brooks-Fournier and Coggeshall, 1981 ). In addition, more than one preganglionic fiber may synapse with a single ganglion neuron. A large number of sympathetic spinal neurons (1000-2000/ganglion) terminate on the ganglia which control the head or thoracic organs and a relatively small number (100-400/ganglion) terminate on ganglia controlling the gut, kidney, and pelvic organs in the rat (Strack et al., 1988 ). The great majority of paravertebral ganglion neurons are adrenergic (Jarvi and Pelto-Huikko, 1990; Tajti et al., 1999 ). They also contain acetylcholine, calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), dopamine-beta-hydroxylase, galanin, neuropeptide Y, nitric oxide, somatostatin, tyrosine hydroxylase, and vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) (Jarvi et al., 1987; Schmitt et al., 1988, Lindh et al., 1989; Jarvi and Pelto-Huikko, 1990; Baffi et al., 1992; Dun et al., 1992, 1993; Benarroch, 1994; Vizzard et al., 1994; Tajti et al., 1999; Zhou and Ling, 1999 ). Although the sympathetic ganglia were formerly accepted merely as relay stations for the transfer of information from the central nervous system to the periphery, it is now known that signals traveling along the preganglionic nerve fibers are distributed, integrated, and/or modified here (deGroat and Saum, 1976; Burnstock et al., 1987; Gibbins et al., 2000; Myers, 2001 ). Some of the preganglionic symptathetic fibers entering the paravertebral ganglia may pass through without a synapse to form the splanchic nerves that lead to prevertebral ganglia (prevertebral plexuses, collateral ganglia) located in prevertebral plexuses of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis. Structurally, the prevertebral ganglia are very similar to the paravertebral ganglia (Gabella, 1995 ). However, there are marked differences in nerve growth factor dependence, neuropeptide content, connectivity and electrophysiological properties (Szurszewski, 1981; Hill et al., 1985; Cassell et al., 1986; Dixon and McKinnon, 1994 ). Neurons of the prevertebral ganglia contain substance P, VIP and enkephalin (Schultzberg, 1983; Herbrecht et al., 1995; Klein and Burden, 1988 ). Axons of sympathetic ganglion neurons are unmyelinated and therefore appear gray when demonstrated by dissection. Some of the axons re-enter the spinal nerves by way of the gray rami communicantes which usually join the nerve just proximal to the white ramus. These are segmentally distributed in every spinal nerve through the ventral and dorsal rami, from C1 to the coccygeal nerve, to sweat glands, smooth muscles of blood vessels, or hair (arrector pili) muscles. Each ganglion neuron gives a postganglionic somatic branch to a single spinal nerve, and every spinal nerve receives gray rami communicantes from the sympathetic chain. When formed by the fusion of more than one ganglion, the ganglion may give and receive as many branches as the segments it contains, e.g., the superior cervical ganglion consists of fibers intended for C1-C4 and consequently gives off four branches to these spinal nerves. Dorsal rami of spinal nerves in humans Dorsal rami of spinal nerves, with the exception of the first two cervical spinal nerves, are smaller than the ventral rami. They supply the muscles, fascia, ligaments, and skin of the dorsal part of the neck and trunk. Dorsal rami divide into a medial and a lateral branch (except for the first cervical, fourth and fifth sacral and the coccygeal nerves). Dorsal rami of the cervical nerves, with the exception of C1, divide into a medial and a lateral branch, both of which innervate the muscles. The dorsal ramus of the C1 nerve (named the suboccipital nerve) is larger than the ventral ramus and may occasionally be absent. The suboccipital nerve supplies the muscles of the suboccipital triangle and the semispinalis capitis. Sometimes it has a cutaneous branch that joins the greater or lesser occipital nerves. The C2 dorsal ramus gives a large medial branch (the greater occipital nerve) and a small lateral branch. The greater occipital nerve supplies the skin of the back of the scalp as far as the vertex of the skull. The lateral branch supplies adjoining muscles. The C3 dorsal ramus has a superficial medial branch, also known as the third occipital nerve, which innervates the skin of lower occipital region, and a deep lateral branch that enters the multifidus muscle. The suboccipital nerve and the medial branches of the C2-C3 dorsal rami are sometimes joined with nerve fiber loops to form the posterior cervical plexus (Cruveilhier) in the posterior cervical region. The dorsal rami of the lower five cervical nerves also divide into medial and lateral branches. The medial branches of C4-C5 run between the semispinalis capitis and the semispinalis cervicis muscles and finish as cutaneous branches; lateral branches reach the longissimus capitis or splenius capitis muscles. The dorsal rami of C7-C8 (and occasionally C5 and C6) do not have cutaneous branches. Lateral branches of C6-C8 dorsal rami supply the iliocostalis cervicis, longissimus cervicis and longissimus capitis muscles; the medial branches supply the multifidus, semispinalis cervicis, and interspinalis muscles (Becser et al., 1998; Zhang et al., 2003 ). The thoracic dorsal rami divide into medial and lateral branches close to the facet joints. The medial branches of the upper thoracic dorsal rami (T1-T6), after traveling through the erector spinae, become superficial and reach the tips of the spinous processes of corresponding vertebrae to innervate the skin. They supply the semispinalis thoracis and multifidus muscles. An anastomosis between the dorsal medial cutaneous branch of T2 with the descending lateral branch of the accessory nerve has been observed (Maigne et al., 1991 ). The lateral branches of the dorsal rami innervate the lateral paravertebral muscles. From T7 to L1 (or L2), this pattern is reversed: the medial branches of these nerves end up at the tip of the spinous processes, supplying the multifidus and longissimus thoracis muscles, and occasionally innervating the skin near the midline; the lateral branches run through, and supply the longissimus thoracis and the iliocostalis muscles, and also give off cutaneous branches that pierce the serratus posterior inferior and latissimus dorsi muscles. The lateral branch of the dorsal ramus of T12 runs over the iliac crest to the ventral part of the gluteal skin. Cervical dorsal rami Thoracic dorsal rami Lumbar dorsal rami The lumbar dorsal rami arise at right angles from the spinal nerves just after their exit from the intervertebral foramina and divide into medial and lateral branches. The medial and lateral branches supply the multifidi and erector spinae muscles, respectively. The medial branches of the lower three lumbar segments give small branches to the skin of the sacral region; the lateral branches of the upper three lumbar dorsal spinal rami give off cutaneous nerves that descend to innervate the skin of the buttock. According to Bogduk et al., (1982), the L1-L4 dorsal rami form three branches: medial, lateral, and intermediate, which are distributed to the multifidi, iliocostalis and longissimus muscles, respectively. The L4 dorsal ramus regularly forms three branches whereas at L1-L3 the lateral and intermediate branches may alternatively arise from a short common stem. The L5 dorsal ramus is much longer than the other lumbar dorsal rami and forms only a medial and an intermediate branch. Sacral dorsal rami The sacral dorsal rami emerge through the dorsal sacral foramina. The upper three dorsal sacral rami divide into medial and lateral branches beneath the multifidi. The medial branches innervate the multifidi. Lateral branches of S1-S3 (S4) and L5 dorsal rami anastomose with each other to form the posterior sacrococcygeal plexus (posterior sacral nerve plexus). Further branches arise from this plexus to form a second series of loops under the gluteus maximus muscle; nerves originating from here pierce this muscle to supply the skin over the lower part of the buttock. The dorsal rami of S4-S5 are small and lie below the multifidi. They unite with each other and with the posterior division of the coccygeal nerve to form loops on the back of the sacrum to supply the skin over the coccyx. Coccygeal dorsal rami The dorsal ramus of the coccygeal nerve is small and does not branch. It communicates with a branch from S5 to supply the skin over the dorsal surface of the coccyx. Ventral rami of spinal nerves in humans The ventral rami originate from the spinal nerves after their emergence from the intervertebral foramina. They supply the muscles, fascia and ligaments of the ventrolateral aspects of the trunk, limbs and perineum, as well as providing the sympathetic and sensory innervation of the skin. The ventral rami are composed of axons from the ventral and dorsal roots of the spinal cord. The ventral ramus of the spinal nerve contains about twice as many axons and a lower proportion of unmyelinated fibers in comparison with the dorsal ramus (Ygge, 1984 ). Each ventral ramus receives a gray ramus communicans from the corresponding sympathetic ganglion. The thoracic and upper two or three lumbar nerves also have a white ramus communicans. Branches from ventral rami of the S2-S4 spinal nerves join the pelvic plexus of the autonomic nervous system. The ventral rami are distributed in a classic segmental pattern in the thoracic region (this pattern is disturbed in the limb enlargement segments). In the thoracic region, each ventral ramus (intercostal nerve) bifurcates into a collateral branch and a lateral cutaneous branch. The collateral branch runs towards the lower rib and ends as the lower anterior cutaneous nerve of the corresponding intercostal space. The lateral cutaneous branch pierces the intercostal muscles and divides into a smaller dorsal and a larger ventral ramus, which supply the skin of the sides and the lateral part of the ventral surface of the body, respectively. The ventral ramus continues ventrally and gives off branches to adjacent muscles and bones to terminate superficially as the anterior cutaneous branch. In all mammals and in many non-mammalian vertebrates, the ventral rami form plexuses and exchange nerve fibers in the upper cervical, lower cervical (brachial), lumbar, sacral and coccygeal regions. Cervical plexus In humans, the cervical plexus is a plexus of the ventral rami of the first four cervical nerves (C1-C4). Each nerve, except for C1, divides into an ascending and a descending branch, which unite with branches of contiguous nerves to form loops. These loops and their branches form the cervical plexus. Each ventral ramus receives one or more gray rami communicantes from the superior cervical ganglion of the sympathetic trunk. The cervical plexus lies ventral to the scalenus medius and levator scapulae muscles, deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle and the internal jugular vein. From this plexus arise cutaneous and muscular branches to the head, neck, and shoulder, and communicating branches to the vagus, hypoglossal and sympathetic nerves. The superficial (cutaneous) branches emerge near the middle of the dorsal border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle (the region known as the punctum nervosum). These divide into ascending and descending branches. The ascending branches are the lesser occipital (C2-C3), great auricular (C2-C3) and transverse cervical (C2-C3) nerves. The descending branches are the supraclavicular (C3-C4) nerves. The deep (muscular and communicating) branches are divided into lateral and medial branches. The lateral branches are to the sternocleidomastoid (C2-C4), trapezius (C3-C4), levator scapulae (C3-C4), and scalenus medius muscles (C3-C4), and communicating branches are to the accessory nerve (C2-C4). The medial branches are to prevertebral muscles (C1-C4), to infrahyoid muscles (C1-C3) (by way of ansa cervicalis) and to the diaphragm by way of the phrenic nerve (C3-C5). Communicating branches to the vagus nerve (C1-C2), hypoglossal nerve (C1-C2), and to the superior cervical sympathetic ganglion (by gray rami communicantes, C1-C4) also arise from the medial branches. Although classical textbooks imply that all the motor input to the trapezius muscle is from the spinal accessory nerve, fibers from the cervical plexus (C3-C4 nerves) have been shown to carry an additional motor supply to trapezius, independent of the accessory nerve (Stacey et al., 1995; Kierner et al., 2001 ). The ansa cervicalis, formerly called ansa hypoglossi, is formed by the union of the ventral rami of the first three cervical nerves through two main roots, the superior and inferior (Olry and Haines, 2002 ). The superior root (descendens hypoglossi) contains fibers from C1. It first travels within the sheath of the hypoglossal nerve and than in the carotid sheath to join the inferior root to form the ansa cervicalis. The inferior root, named the descending cervical nerve, contains fibers from C2-C3 spinal nerves. It descends on the dorsolateral side of the internal jugular vein. The ansa cervicalis is located deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle and overlies or may sometimes lie within the carotid sheath, usually where the superior belly of the omohyoid muscle crosses over the internal jugular vein (Tubbs et al., 2005 ). Sometimes the ansa is located superior (short ansa) or inferior (long ansa) to the omohyoid muscle (Caliot and Dumont, 1983 ). The branches of ansa cervicalis innervate the infrahyoid muscles. The ansa cervicalis is usually in a ′concentrated′ form, characterized by thick nerve trunks constituting a solitary arch from which one or two branches for the infrahyoid muscles emerge. Rarely, it has a ′diffuse′ form characterized by finer nerve trunks in the form of a plexus (Poviraev and Chernikov, 1967 ). The phrenic nerve usually arises from C3-C5 nerves approximately at the mid-level of the thyroid cartilage. It gives off sensory fibers to mediastinal pleura and pierces the diaphragm to supply it on the caudal surface. Sometimes, an accessory phrenic nerve is present as a contribution to the phrenic nerve from the ventral ramus of C5, derived as a branch from the nerve to the subclavius muscle.
